title: Wayfinding: A simple concept, a complex process
research_question: To examine the motivations for investigating wayfinding, discuss the associated principles and factors involved from different research perspectives, and review the approaches used to date in the modelling of wayfinding in various contexts.

participants.description: Humans navigating built environments, including diverse populations such as people with disabilities, first-time users of transportation hubs, and individuals from different cultural backgrounds, as studied in the reviewed literature.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Built environments, particularly transportation hubs (airports, train/bus stations, malls), cities, and buildings; wayfinding cues (signs, maps, landmarks, paths, edges, districts, nodes, color, light).

measures.construct: Passenger perception of airport level of service
Spatial navigation skills and spatial abilities
Mental rotation, spatial perception, dynamic spatial ability
Conception of space and spatial relations
Performance in spatial and navigational tasks
Calming effect, focus on tasks, awareness, direction to destination
Flow of people in a building

findings.consequent: Passenger perception of airport level of service
findings.quote: Surveys have shown that wayfinding is regarded by passengers as the third most important variable in terms of level of service

findings.antecedent: Ability to form a suitable cognitive map of the environment
findings.quote: Successful spatial orientation occurs when a person can form a suitable cognitive map of the environment
Path distance and travel time have been proven to be the most important factors in route choice.
When there is no obvious correct route choice, the route that will minimize mental and physical efforts is chosen.

findings.antecedent: Least angle strategy (turning as late as possible, maintaining target direction)
findings.consequent: Cognitive effort in navigating and wayfinding
findings.quote: Least angle: people minimize the cognitive effort needed in navigating and wayfinding by turning as late as possible.

findings.antecedent: Initial segment strategy (focus on initial portions of route, prefer longer straight initial segments)
findings.quote: Initial segment: people focus disproportionately on the initial portions of a route and prefer routes with longer straight initial segments

findings.mechanism: minimizing potential risk of getting lost
findings.quote: Least number of turns: routes with the least number of turns are chosen because each turn made allows for a potential risk of getting lost.

findings.antecedent: Fine-to-course strategy (plan to region, then specific route)
findings.quote: Fine-to-course: people plan a route to the region containing the destination, and only once inside that region do they determine a specific route.

findings.antecedent: Using verbal directions instead of or in addition to maps
findings.consequent: Formation of spatial orientation and wayfinding success
findings.quote: Using verbal directions instead of or in addition to maps can cause the formation of spatial orientation, and hence wayfinding to go awry
people who use a language with more differentiation perceive reality differently from those who use a language with less differentiation

findings.consequent: Spatial navigation skills and spatial abilities
findings.quote: Differences exist in the spatial navigation skills and spatial abilities of males and females.

findings.consequent: Performance in spatial activities in wayfinding
findings.quote: Men perform better in spatial activities in wayfinding.

findings.consequent: Accuracy in navigating tasks when directional information is given
findings.quote: Men are more accurate in navigating tasks when directional information is given.

findings.consequent: Preference for distal cues (e.g., hill lines) for orientation and direction
findings.quote: Men prefer and rely on distal cues (e.g. hill lines) to provide information on orientation and direction.

findings.consequent: Scores in mental rotation, spatial perception tests, and dynamic spatial ability
findings.quote: Men score significantly higher in mental rotation, spatial perception tests and dynamic spatial ability.
Women show greater spatial anxiety than men.
Higher anxiety has a negative impact on navigational ability and spatial performance.

findings.consequent: Preference for exact, pinpoint cues (e.g., landmarks) to identify visual scene and form spatial orientation
findings.quote: Women prefer exact, pinpoint cues (e.g. landmarks) to identify a visual scene and form spatial orientation.
Women have better object memory and object-location.
Women tend to adapt more easily to changing route instructions than men.

findings.consequent: Conception of space and spatial relations
findings.quote: Cultural backgrounds are responsible for the differences in how space and spatial relations are conceived.

findings.consequent: Perception and thinking about the world
findings.quote: Different languages structure experience differently, and people who speak different languages perceive and think about the world quite differently.
People who use a language with more differentiation perceive reality differently to people who use a language with less differentiation.

findings.antecedent: Differences in vocabulary, terminology, geographical style, cultural meaning of terms, conversation style
findings.quote: Differences in vocabulary and terminology, geographical style, cultural meaning of terms, conversation style impact on cognitive mapping and spatial cognition.

findings.antecedent: Instructions given in a relative frame of reference
findings.quote: People perform better at wayfinding tasks when they are given their instructions in a relative frame of reference.

findings.antecedent: Instructions given in an absolute reference frame
findings.consequent: Stops and deviations to find a destination
findings.quote: More stops and deviations were needed to find a destination when people were given instructions in the absolute reference frame.

findings.consequent: Performance in spatial and navigational tasks
findings.quote: Testosterone, or the exposure to testosterone, results in increased performance in spatial and navigational tasks.

findings.antecedent: Women in mid-luteal phase of menstrual cycle (high oestrogen levels)
findings.quote: Poorer performance occurs when women are in the mid-luteal phase of the menstrual cycle and oestrogen levels are high.

findings.antecedent: More pronounced right hemisphere on males
findings.mechanism: attributed to better performance in spatial tasks
findings.quote: More pronounced right hemisphere on males is attributed to better performance in spatial tasks.

findings.antecedent: Grid configurations of cities or city block matrices
findings.quote: Grid configurations of cities or city block matrices are easier to comprehend.
Landmarks make wayfinding easier.

findings.antecedent: Placement of landmarks at decision points
findings.quote: The placement of landmarks at decision points affect cognitive wayfinding strategies and facilitate orientation.

findings.antecedent: Landmark salience (contrast with environment in attributes, status, or spatial location)
findings.quote: For a landmark to be salient, it must contrast with the environment in either its attributes... or its spatial location

findings.consequent: Calming effect, focus on visual/mental tasks, awareness, direction to destination
findings.quote: Cool colours are calming and help people focus on visual and mental tasks. Cool colours can increase awareness and help direct people to a destination.
It has been shown that cool-coloured walls are seen as more navigable.

findings.consequent: Focus people outwards, awareness, perception of space, use as landmarks
findings.quote: Warm colours focus people outwards and increase their awareness. The use of warm colours allows people to more easily perceive the space and it has been shown that warm colours can be effectively used as landmarks
Indoor lighting directly effects people's emotions, memory, perceptual-orientation and problem-solving abilities.
Spaces with low brightness levels are perceived negatively compared to other brightness levels.

findings.antecedent: Increases in brightness level of a space
findings.quote: Increases in the brightness level of a space positively correlated with positive perception of the space.

findings.antecedent: Use of cool colours and high brightness levels
findings.quote: The use of cool colours and high brightness levels help people to be spatially orientated.
Maps are used to acquire spatial knowledge, especially survey representations which usually require a long time to acquire via route navigation alone.

findings.antecedent: Map learning aligned with initial orientation of the map
findings.quote: Map learning leads to superior performance only when aligned with the initial orientation of the map.

findings.consequent: Improved wayfinding performance and spatial learning in an unfamiliar building
findings.quote: There is mixed evidence regarding the existence of a positive relationship between access to floor maps and an improved wayfinding performance and spatial learning in an unfamiliar building.

findings.consequent: Wayfinding ease (to compensate for complex floor plans)
findings.quote: Signage is used to compensate for complex floor plans in order to make wayfinding easier.
Signs placed at decision points improve the wayfinding performance.
Direction signage has been shown to have the greatest effect on wayfinding and is relied upon heavily in order to make decisions regarding wayfinding.
In some settings, signage enhances wayfinding and reduces confusion and stress; however, in other cases, it is ignored or found to be confusing.
Textual signage has been shown to be more effective than graphical signage in reducing wayfinding errors such as wrong turns and backtracks.

findings.consequent: Flow of people in a building
findings.quote: Graphic signage though has been shown to allow for a faster flow of people in a building.
route planning is a sequential and hierarchical process with clear distinctions between route planning and action planning.
route planning was found to always contain two parts: a behaviour component... and a location/landmark specifier

findings.consequent: Ease of wayfinding in a terminal
findings.quote: Higher index values indicate easier wayfinding in the terminal
V, the measure proposed by Braaksma et al. (1980) gave the smallest result.

findings.antecedent: Weighted Visibility Index (VTw, Tosic and Babic, 1984)
findings.quote: The weighted model by Tosic and Babic (1984), VTw, gave the largest value, most likely due to the exclusion of irrelevant routes.

findings.antecedent: Dada and Wirasinghe (1999) model (VD) vs. Tosic and Babic (1984) model (VT)
findings.quote: They found that the difference between the results from VT and VD can be largely attributed to signage.

findings.mechanism: decrease in accuracy of cognitive map
findings.quote: Increases in the ICD result in an increase in wayfinding difficulty

findings.consequent: Accuracy of the cognitive map formed
findings.quote: Increases in the ICD result in an increase in wayfinding difficulty due to the decrease in the accuracy of the cognitive map formed

findings.consequent: Mean time to find a destination, average number of wrong turns, average number of backtracking incidents
findings.quote: It also increases the mean time to find a destination, the average number of wrong terms and the average number of backtracking incidents.

findings.consequent: Accuracy of the cognitive map and wayfinding performance
findings.quote: Incremental differences in ICD are shown to have significant impact on reported measures of the accuracy of the cognitive map and the wayfinding performance.

findings.antecedent: Topological complexity of a built environment
findings.quote: the topological complexity of a built environment is an important variable that has a large influence on the overall legibility of an environment.
Peponis et al. (1990) found that correlations existed between the measures of a building's spatial configuration and indicators of the wayfinding performance.

findings.antecedent: Travel patterns of participants over time
findings.mechanism: spatial learning adapts to larger organization characteristics
findings.quote: travel patterns began to correlate strongly with 'integration' and other space syntax global measures

findings.antecedent: Residents' sketch maps of their neighbourhood
findings.consequent: 'Integration' values of streets in the real environment
findings.quote: the sketch maps showed similar 'integration' values as the streets in the real environment.

findings.antecedent: Novice vs. expert travellers in a complex building
findings.quote: novices chose travel paths that were more visually connected and 'integrated' than the expert travellers

findings.antecedent: Wayfinding use of axial lines and nodes
findings.quote: Haq (1999) found the existence of a relationship between the wayfinding use of axial lines and nodes and their space syntax integration values.

mechanisms: Decision-making, decision execution, and information processing (environmental perception and cognition) as core wayfinding processes.
Formation of cognitive maps and spatial orientation.
Implicit strategies to minimize mental and physical efforts in route choice.
Individual differences in spatial ability, language, culture, gender, and biological factors influencing wayfinding.
Environmental elements (paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks) providing cues for navigation.
Maps and signs serving as wayfinding devices for orientation and direction.
Spatial processing abilities, familiarity with the environment, and environmental complexity influencing wayfinding performance.
Sequential and hierarchical nature of route planning.
Visibility of sight lines influencing ease of wayfinding.
Topological complexity of floor plans impacting legibility and wayfinding difficulty.
Spatial configuration and integration (space syntax) affecting travel patterns and spatial knowledge acquisition.
moderators: Biological factors (e.g., testosterone levels, menstrual cycle phase)
implementation_implications: Understanding wayfinding principles allows for designing spaces that enable quick and efficient navigation, especially in transport terminals and during emergencies.
Improved wayfinding design can increase efficiency and effectiveness of public buildings for people with disabilities.
Correct application of wayfinding principles reduces frustration and improves customer experience.
Wayfinding design can contribute to an area's or city's sense of identity.
Design should prioritize equitable use, flexibility, simple and intuitive use, perceptible information, tolerance for error, low physical effort, and appropriate size and space.

Wayfinding systems in airports can direct passenger flow, provide correct information for disabled passengers, facilitate evacuation, reduce tangible costs, and decrease passenger stress and frustration.
Balancing wayfinding facilities for essential navigation with elements guiding passengers to retail outlets is important for airport operators.
Technological developments like mobile apps can enhance wayfinding by tracking user position and providing directions.

A summary of some cognitively based computer models that simulate learning and problem solving in spatial networks
The VI was initially proposed by Braaksma et al. (1980) as an attempt to relate the ease of wayfinding to the value of available sight lines in an environment

limitations: Cognitive models have a major limitation in determining the reasons or intentions of subjects' actions.
Mathematical models (e.g., VI, ICD) primarily focus on environmental aspects and do not account for human factors in wayfinding.

Space syntax models ignore some important human and environmental factors, such as individual differences, superficial environmental aspects (colors, patterns, textures), and metrics like distance and direction.
Current wayfinding research lacks a holistic model that integrates both human and environmental factors to determine their relative importance.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Wayfinding is a complex, multi-faceted cognitive process involving perception, memory, decision-making, and action, influenced by environmental, individual, and task-related factors.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper describes wayfinding as a complex process involving the perception of environmental information, its cognitive processing into spatial knowledge, and the subsequent use of this knowledge for decision-making and action.

steps.from_construct: Environmental features (e.g., landmarks, signs, spatial layout)

steps.to_construct: Formation and updating of cognitive maps/spatial knowledge
Wayfinding outcome (e.g., success, efficiency, perceived ease)
